Office of Public Affairs | Justice Department Announces Final Rule Allowing Federal Firearms Licensees to Voluntarily Use NICS for Employee Background Checks | United States Department of Justice Skip to main content Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. DOJ Menu U.S. Department of Justice About The Attorney General
Justice Department Announces Final Rule Allowing Federal Firearms Licensees to Voluntarily Use NICS for Employee Background Checks
Today, the Department of Justice announced a final rule authorizing Federal Firearms Licensees (FFLs) to voluntarily use the FBI's National Instant Criminal Background Check System (NICS) to conduct background checks on certain current and prospective employees.
“Firearms dealers deserve the confidence of knowing their employees are right with the law,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “This common-sense change delivers quick and clear background checks for firearms dealers based on the latest FBI information. The Trump Administration will always protect the Second Amendment and the rights of law-abiding gun owners.”
“Under the leadership of President Trump and Attorney General Blanche, this FBI will always protect the Second Amendment and the rights of law-abiding gun owners,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “This is a common-sense change that appropriately expedites and clarifies the background check process for firearms dealers, and I want to thank our partners for working with us to make it happen.”
The final rule implements a provision of the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act , which directed the Attorney General to issue these regulations. Participation is optional for FFLs and requires the written consent of the employee.
Under the final rule, an FFL may submit Firearm Handler Background Checks (FHCs) of eligible employees. Eligible employees include firearm handlers, employees of licensed manufacturers who have access to unfinished firearm components or manufacturing tools, and independent contractors or agents whose employment duties for an FFL allow them access to firearms, ammunition, or their manufacturing components. Those listed as responsible persons of FFLs are not eligible employees because they already undergo background checks through the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. Until now, Department of Justice regulations prohibited FFLs from contacting NICS for any purpose other than a proposed firearm transfer.
NICS will search the same databases it does for a firearm transfer: the NICS Indices, the National Crime Information Center, and the Interstate Identification Index. The FFL will receive a NICS Transaction Number and one of three responses: "Pass," "Pending," or "Did Not Pass." FFLs will not receive any of the subject’s underlying record information. A "Did Not Pass" response does not prohibit an FFL from employing the person in a position that does not involve access to firearms or ammunition. Generally, an FFL may conduct one FHC per eligible employee every 12 months, unless the FFL has reasonable cause to believe the employee has become subject to a potentially prohibiting event. The FBI will not charge a fee for these checks.
A subject whose FHC received a "Did Not Pass" response may request the reason for the response and may appeal that response in the same manner and to the same extent as a person who is denied a firearm transfer.
The final rule addresses applicable public comments received on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that was published in December 2024. The final rule takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives will issue separate guidance to FFLs on how to document FHCs.
Jald Jensen, 73, of Panama City, and previously

Kenya’s Phoebe Okowa elected to International Court of Justice
The UN has elected five judges to the International Court of Justice, including Kenya’s Phoebe Okowa, who has secured a full nine-year term starting in February 2027.
Okowa won 183 votes in the General Assembly and 13 in the Security Council. She is a professor of public international law at Queen Mary University of London and has served on the UN’s International Law Commission since 2021.
The other elected judges are Dapo Akande of the United Kingdom, François Alabrune of France, Mahmoud Daifallah Hmoud of Jordan and Rena Lee of Singapore.
The International Court of Justice, based in The Hague, settles legal disputes between states and issues advisory opinions on legal questions referred to it by authorised
Based in The Hague, the Court comprises 15 judges serving nine-year terms, with five seats coming up for election every three years.
No two judges may be nationals of the same State.
Candidates must secure an absolute majority in both the 193-member Assembly and the 15-member Council, which vote independently by secret ballot.
The veto does not apply, and multiple rounds of voting may be necessary.

sources.title: Rwanda's army team removed from BAL after US sanctions, NBA says - BBC News
sources.text:
Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, Rwanda's army team APR came third in the Basketball Africa League last year By Basillioh Rukanga Published 4 November 2026
The National Basketball Association (NBA) says it removed Rwanda's army team from its African league because of US sanctions imposed on the country in March.
The NBA had previously said the Rwandan army-funded Armée Patriotique Rwandaise (APR) club would not participate in the 2026 Basketball Africa League (BAL).
However this is the first time the NBA has revealed the reasons behind the APR's removal.
The association was responding to complaints by two US senators, who sent a letter asking them to reconsider their partnership with the Rwandan team. The US placed sanctions on the Rwandan army, accusing it of fuelling the conflict in the Democratic Republic of Congo in March.
The senators said the NBA risked "becoming complicit in sportswashing by accepting money from a Rwandan government that systematically abuses human rights".
Last week, the US also imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its support for the M23 rebel group which has seized control of large parts of eastern DR Congo. Rwanda denies backing the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.
Rwanda is an official BAL partner and pays the league to host its finals at the 10,000-seat BK Arena in the capital, Kigali.
What is the Basketball Africa League? Published 14 May 2021
The evidence that shows Rwanda is backing rebels in DR Congo Published 29 January 2025
In the letter to the NBA dated 23 October, Democratic Senator Jeffrey Merkley and Republican counterpart Marsha Blackburn gave the association until 2 November to give a written response regarding its continued partnership with Rwanda.
"What is the NBA red line for accepting money from foreign governments that commit human rights abuses?" the senators asked.
Among other queries, they also questioned how the association could "reconcile its continued partnership with Rwanda with its purported commitment to justice".
In its response, NBA deputy commissioner Mark Tatum said the Rwandan team "had been withdrawn" from the BAL following the sanctions imposed earlier in the year, American sports website ESPN reports.
The NBA said the APR basketball club would remain barred while the US sanctions are in place.
The APR is one of Rwanda's top basketball teams and represented the country in the BAL in 2024 and 2025, when it came third. It was replaced by the RSSB Tigers this year.
The BAL is a pan-African basketball league established and co-organised by the NBA and the basketball's world governing body Fiba.
It is a professional league featuring 12 club teams from across the continent.
Rwanda has hosted all but one of the league's final and playoff matches since the inaugural match in 2021.
The NBA reportedly receives millions of dollars annually from the country for the marketing and partnership rights.
DR Congo has repeatedly condemned Rwanda's high-profile international sports deals, including with the NBA, European football clubs and Formula 1, asking them to end their campaigns.
It argues that these help Rwanda clean up its global image, while the conflict continues in eastern DR Congo.

sources.title: The Daily View: Sanctions pragmatism collides with shadow fleet reality :: Lloyd's List
sources.text:
The Daily View: Sanctions pragmatism collides with shadow fleet reality
Your latest edition of Lloyd’s List’s Daily View — the essential briefing on the stories shaping shipping
Richard Meade @Lloydslisted [email protected]
WHEN US Energy Secretary Chris Wright raised the prospect of easing sanctions on shadow fleet tankers at the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh this week, even delegates were caught off guard.
His comments do not amount to policy, yet, and no detail has emerged. But Lloyd’s List has confirmed Wright’s comments first hand with delegates who heard him speak in the room. The logic was clear enough. With tanker rates at extraordinary levels, why leave potentially useful ships stranded on sanctions lists when Donald Trump wants more unsanctioned oil moving?
The problem is that removing a tanker from a US blacklist does not magically turn a 20-year-old shadow vessel into acceptable mainstream tonnage.
Sanctions relief does not make these ships safer, and allowing them back would send the “wrong signal” to owners that have invested heavily in safety, compliance and transparency.
Most major charterers will still baulk at elderly vessels lacking recognised class, International Group P&I cover or transparent ownership histories. UK and EU sanctions would remain. Banks, insurers and charterers would still have compliance concerns.
That considerably reduces the headline capacity potentially available.
US-sanctioned crude tanker tonnage amounts to almost 80m dwt, equivalent to 16% of the global fleet, while Lloyd’s List Intelligence identifies 1,470 tankers facilitating sanctioned Iranian, Russian and Venezuelan trades.
But theoretical tonnage is not commercially usable capacity. Fewer than 25 sanctioned VLCCs could realistically return to trade without further waivers or overcoming age-related barriers.
A more plausible application might be using rehabilitated vessels as Middle East Gulf shuttles, carrying unsanctioned crude through Hormuz for transfer to mainstream tonnage. Even that is unlikely to make a significant dent in freight rates while heightened Middle East war risk remains the primary driver .
The bigger issue is what the proposal says about sanctions policy.
Washington has already temporarily loosened restrictions on Russian diesel in a deal that will do little to resolve the underlying causes of the diesel shortages.
Rehabilitating shadow tankers would take that flawed pragmatism considerably further, while putting the US increasingly at odds with European allies seeking to strand precisely the same fleet.
Europe is trying to undermine the shadow fleet’s business model. Washington is considering putting part of it back to work.
That contradiction points to an uncomfortable truth: when sanctions enforcement collides with energy security and inflation, priorities can change remarkably quickly.
Richard Meade Editor-in-chief, Lloyd’s List

sources.title: Joo Chiat vs Haji Lane: What does it take for independent shops to survive? - CNA Lifestyle
sources.text:
Joo Chiat vs Haji Lane: What makes a shopping neighbourhood work for retailers?
Haji Lane offers visibility, while Joo Chiat provides room to linger. But for Singapore’s independent retailers, neither foot traffic nor a distinctive setting guarantees a sustainable business.
(Art: Chern Ling; photos: Beau, In Good Company, Singapore Tourism Board)
Chin Chih Lin 05 Nov 2026 07:31AM (Updated: 05 Nov 2026 07:35AM) Bookmark Bookmark Share WhatsApp Telegram Facebook Twitter Email LinkedIn Set CNA as your preferred source on Google Add CNA as a trusted source to help Google better understand and surface our content in search results. Read a summary of this article on FAST. Get bite-sized news via a new cards interface. Give it a try. Click here to return to FAST Tap here to return to FAST FAST For independent retailers, a busy street can be a double-edged sword. More foot traffic means more potential customers, but not everyone who walks through the door intends to buy, and high rents make that gap costly.
That tension runs through two of Singapore’s best-known independent retail enclaves. Joo Chiat and Haji Lane both offer what malls struggle to replicate: shophouse character, strong identities and a mix of shops, cafes and concepts that makes shopping feel like discovery.
But they are developing differently. Joo Chiat is becoming a neighbourhood for lingering, with brands building spaces that invite people to stay, while Haji Lane’s tourist crowds have drawn in photobooths and food concepts alongside the fashion and vintage stores that made its name.
For retailers, the question is the same in both places: Can the numbers work, with the cost of running a physical store still climbing?
For local home and lifestyle brand Sojao, Joo Chiat was a natural fit for its flagship before the neighbourhood became the buzzy lifestyle destination it is today.
Co-founder Jan Tan grew up near the area, as did fellow co-founder Priscilla Tan (not related). “In fact, my parents used to run a hawker stall nearby at Dunman Food Centre,” said Jac Tan.
The brand launched online in 2018 and has operated its 1,400 sq ft flagship at 251 Joo Chiat Road since November 2021. Its second outlet, at New Bahru, opened in June 2024 and is just under 1,000 sq ft.
Joo Chiat’s residential character, historic shophouses and independent spirit were the draw. So was cost – mall rents can be steep, and often come with long opening hours.
“We wanted the store to feel like part of a neighbourhood rather than simply another shop in a mall,” Tan added. “We felt a more experiential, rather than transactional, environment would suit the brand.”
Its customers include residents, Singaporeans making a dedicated trip (some customers even call for directions, as the store is a little far from an MRT station) and tourists, with Chinese visitors particularly strong. The brand does not track an exact local-to-tourist split.
Others find Sojao by accident. Someone might come for brunch, wander into a few independent shops and end up in the store. For a brand selling bedding, being found in person matters. Customers can read about the softness of organic cotton online, but nothing replaces touching it.
“The neighbourhood itself becomes part of the experience,” said Tan. Food and beverage businesses give people a reason to stay for hours, while fashion, design, beauty and wellness shops give them more to discover. Independent businesses benefit from one another rather than having to attract every customer alone.
Homegrown fashion label In Good Company is making a similar bet.
Opened in July, its three-storey, 3,000 sq ft Joo Chiat flagship retains the shophouse’s original brick walls, timber flooring, exposed beams and spiral staircase, with warm finishes and woven textures lending a more residential feel. It combines fashion with hospitality, design and collaborations, including Miura, a Japanese tea and wagashi space by the team behind Paaru.

sources.title: Traffic gridlock at Malaysia-Singapore causeway after Woodlands blackout
sources.text:
URL Source: https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/southeast-asia/article/3373311/traffic-gridlock-malaysia-singapore-causeway-after-woodlands-blackout

Published Time: 2026-11-04T23:41:20+08:00

Markdown Content:
A massive power outage at the Woodlands checkpoint in [Singapore](https://www.scmp.com/topics/singapore?module=inline&pgtype=article) caused a heavy traffic jam on most major roads leading to the Malaysian checkpoint in Johor Bahru on Wednesday.

Although all counters were operating at optimum level at the Bangunan Sultan Iskandar Customs, Immigration and Quarantine complex in the southern state of Johor, the jam lasted for many hours due to a build-up of vehicles from the Singapore side.

It is learnt that the issue started at about noon on the Singapore side. A Malaysian home ministry official said the situation was worsened by a truck heading to Singapore experiencing mechanical failure.

It remains unclear what caused the power outage in Singapore.

Authorities were doing their best to resolve the congestion, including opening additional lanes to clear immigration.

Additional police personnel have also been deployed around the customs complex and major access roads to manage the peak-hour rush of workers returning from Singapore.

Among the major roads affected were Jalan Tebrau, Jalan Skudai and Jalan Lingkaran Dalam. At about 9pm, the travel time into Johor Bahru was 32 minutes while travel into Singapore from Johor Bahru stood at one hour and 10 minutes.

![Image 1: Traffic on the Malaysia-Singapore causeway on Wednesday night. Photo: The Star](https://img.i-scmp.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=contain,width=1024,format=auto/sites/default/files/d8/images/canvas/2026/11/04/e94681c0-fb36-4fb4-9507-346ed6a9df71_34160d74.jpg)

Traffic on the Malaysia-Singapore causeway on Wednesday night. Photo: The Star

Singapore’s Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) said on social media that travellers planning to enter Singapore via Woodlands checkpoint should expect delays.

It said that two vehicles had broken down near the international boundary along the causeway towards Singapore, blocking one out of three lanes.

Heavy traffic was expected at Singapore’s Woodlands and Tuas checkpoints during the coming Deepavali long weekend, ICA said on Sunday.

Travellers should also expect longer waiting times during peak travel periods, as ICA has stepped up security checks at all checkpoints since February 28 in view of the “heightened global security environment, particularly recent developments in the Middle East”.

During the recent Singapore school holidays from September 4 to September 14, more than 6.1 million travellers crossed both land checkpoints, with the volume peaking at more than 599,000 on September 4.

This set a record, ICA said, surpassing the previous peak of more than 598,000 crossings on June 19. Car travellers departing during peak hours experienced waiting times of up to three hours for immigration clearance, due to traffic jams from Malaysia.

_This article was first published by_[_The Star_](https://www.thestar.com.my/news/nation/2026/11/04/power-outage-at-woodlands-checkpoint-triggers-massive-causeway-gridlock)

_Additional reporting by CNA_

U.S. Sanctions Law Firm, Shipping Agents and Nine Vessels in Iran Shadow Fleet Crackdown
The United States has imposed a new round of sanctions targeting a law firm, shipping agents and nine vessels accused of helping Iran move oil and other commodities through international markets, expanding Washington’s crackdown on the networks supporting Tehran’s shadow fleet.
The U.S. Treasury Department announced the measures Wednesday as part of Operation Economic Outcast, an ongoing campaign aimed at cutting off Iran’s remaining sources of revenue amid the continuing conflict in the Middle East.
At the center of the latest action is Karnakis and Karnakis, a law firm operating in Panama and Greece that Treasury says has spent years establishing shell companies used to conceal the ownership of vessels transporting Iranian petroleum, petrochemicals and steel.
According to Treasury, the firm helped register shipping companies responsible for moving hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of Iranian commodities, including vessels connected to previously sanctioned entities.
The law firm also played a key role in establishing the corporate network behind Iranian liquefied petroleum gas magnate Seyed Asadoollah Emamjomeh, whose shipping operations have transported hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of Iranian LPG and crude oil.
Treasury sanctioned the firm and five associated individuals, accusing them of helping obscure the true ownership of companies involved in Iranian commodity shipments.
The action represents a broader effort to target not just the vessels carrying sanctioned cargo, but also the legal, corporate and logistical services that allow shadow fleet operators to function.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that those supporting Iranian shipping operations would face consequences, saying, “if you are supporting the Iranian regime, we will find you and sanction you.”
Seven Cargo Ships and Two Support Vessels Targeted
The latest designations also include Roxette Maritime Shipping and Trading S.A., a Panama- and Greece-based company for which Karnakis and Karnakis serves as corporate agent.
Treasury identified Roxette as the operator and ship manager of seven Panama-flagged cargo vessels: ANEMOS, GLORIS, PRIDE, DESTINY, FLAMINGO 1, HARMONY and PRINCE.
Three of those vessels — ANEMOS, GLORIS and PRIDE — carried Iranian-origin goods, including petrochemicals and steel products, within the past year, according to Treasury.
All seven vessels were identified as blocked property under the new sanctions.
The department also targeted two shipping agencies accused of facilitating Iranian cargo movements through international ports.
Singapore-based Amigoz Singapore PTE. Ltd. allegedly provided port services for an Iranian light crude shipment connected to Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company, which Treasury says helps channel billions of dollars’ worth of commodities to Iranian military entities.
Amigoz was also linked to vessels associated with the shipping network of Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani and provided bunkering services to the previously sanctioned shadow fleet vessel ZIXUAN.
Meanwhile, Dubai-based Whales Shipping Line LLC was sanctioned for its involvement with Amigoz. Treasury said Whales had also acted as a shipping agent for a sanctioned trading company involved in purchasing tens of millions of dollars’ worth of Iranian petrochemicals.
Two UAE-flagged support vessels owned by Whales, WHALES DIAMOND and WHALES PEARL, were identified as blocked property.
The measures are the latest under Operation Economic Outcast, launched on August 24 as part of the Trump administration’s campaign to isolate Iran economically.
The effort has increasingly focused on the international network of ship managers, brokers, port agents, financial institutions and corporate service providers that support Iranian oil exports and sanctions evasion.
Wednesday’s announcement also included a financial enforcement component.
Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) said it was working with European partners, including authorities in Greece, to investigate a Greek bank’s potential connections to Iran and its proxies.
The agency said it had issued its first administrative subpoena under a provision of the Bank Secrecy Act as part of that investigation, along with additional requests for information concerning banks’ relationships with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions.
The latest sanctions come as Washington continues applying military and economic pressure on Iran, including efforts to restrict its maritime trade through the Strait of Hormuz.

claims.text: On October 29, 2026, OFAC issued Iran General License FF-1, signed by Director Bradley T. Smith, authorizing the wind down of transactions prohibited by the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations (31 CFR part 560) that involve International Development Bank for Investment and Finance (a.k.a. Iraq Development Bank) or any entity in which it owns, directly or indirectly, a 50 percent or greater interest, through 12:01 a.m. eastern standard time, December 1, 2026.

Effective October 29, 2026, Iran General License FF-1 replaced and superseded in its entirety General License No. FF dated October 15, 2026; under FF-1 any payment to a blocked person must be made into a blocked account in accordance with the ITSR, and the license does not authorize transactions involving any person blocked under the ITSR other than the bank and its 50-percent-or-greater-owned entities.

On October 21, 2026, OFAC issued Iran General License GG authorizing the wind down of transactions involving Karnakis and Karnakis, and Iran General License HH authorizing wind-down activities, limited safety and environmental transactions, and the offloading of cargo involving certain persons or vessels blocked on October 21, 2026.

letters.subject: Source request: OFAC Iran General License FF-1 and related designations
letters.body:
Dear US Department of Justice,

We are PLAIN., an independent, advertising-free Swiss news site reporting internationally (plain-news.ch). Our investigative desk is examining US OFAC amendments to Iran sanctions licensing, including Iran General License FF-1 of October 29, 2026, and the designations and wind-down licenses issued on October 21, 2026. This research is AI-assisted and every text is reviewed by a human editor. We would appreciate your help in clarifying the following specific points.

1. Under General License FF-1, which Iranian entities are now restricted, and does the license cover only the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance (also known as Iraq Development Bank) and entities in which it holds a direct or indirect 50 percent or greater interest?

2. How does FF-1's requirement that any payment to a blocked person be made into a blocked account in accordance with the ITSR affect international trade transactions that would otherwise fall within the authorized wind-down through 12:01 a.m. eastern standard time on December 1, 2026?

3. What specific transactions remain prohibited under FF-1, given that it does not authorize transactions involving any person blocked under the ITSR other than the bank and its 50-percent-or-greater-owned entities?

4. What is the stated basis for the October 21, 2026 SDN additions under Executive Order 13902 of Karnakis Kosmas Ioanis, Karnakis Kosmas Konstantinos, Karnakis Kosmas Sofianos, Ortega Jones Pedro, Ortega Jones Roberto, Amigoz Singapore Pte. Ltd. and Karnakis and Karnakis, and how do General Licenses GG and HH relate to those designations?

5. What was the specific effect of FF-1 replacing and superseding General License FF of October 15, 2026 in its entirety on transactions already underway?

We will publish your reply, either in full or as a summary, as you prefer. If anything we have stated is factually wrong, please tell us so that we can correct it. We would be grateful for an answer by 8 November 2026.

Sincerely,

PLAIN. Investigative desk
desk@plain-news.ch
